scenes.visual: Title card 'Pushed From the Source' over a plant cartoon with a BLUE xylem line and an AMBER phloem line side by side. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP (shared by both films, figures and take-homes): xylem and water BLUE (blue droplets), phloem AMBER, sucrose GOLD hexagons, tension RED, air pale GREY; pressure shown as a vertical gauge with a zero line, positive above (amber when phloem), negative below in RED. Symbols on screen: Ψ, Ψ_s, Ψ_p. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Sugar made in a leaf ends up in a root below it and a shoot tip above it. What moves it both ways, with no heart and nothing pulling?
scenes.visual: A mature leaf glows; GOLD hexagons leave it, some travelling down an AMBER line to the roots and some up to a shoot tip. A crossed-out heart icon and a crossed-out RED tension gauge appear, then a question mark.
scenes.narration: Sugar made in a leaf ends up in a root below it and a shoot tip above it. What moves it both ways, with no heart and nothing pulling?

scenes.tts: Water in the xylem is pulled toward dry air. Sugar rides in the phloem, in living sieve tubes. And nothing evaporates at a root to pull it.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's BLUE column rising under a RED gauge. Beside it an AMBER tube made of living cells (cartoon cells with cytoplasm) labelled 'sieve tube', ending in a root tip with no vapour puff.
scenes.narration: Water in the xylem is pulled toward dry air. Sugar rides in the phloem, in living sieve tubes. And nothing evaporates at a root to pull it.

scenes.tts: In nineteen thirty, Ernst Munch pictured two bulbs joined by a tube. Each is wrapped in a membrane that lets water through but holds sugar back. Both sit in water.
scenes.caption: In 1930, Ernst Münch pictured two bulbs joined by a tube. Each is wrapped in a membrane that lets water through but holds sugar back. Both sit in water.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Ernst Münch, 1930'. Two round bulbs, A and B, joined by a horizontal AMBER tube, sitting in a BLUE water bath. Each bulb outline is dashed, label 'membrane: water passes, sugar does not'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: In 1930, Ernst Münch pictured two bulbs joined by a tube. Each is wrapped in a membrane that lets water through but holds sugar back. Both sit in water.

scenes.tts: Put strong sugar solution in one bulb. The sugar lowers its water potential, so water rushes in by osmosis. The pressure inside rises.
scenes.visual: GOLD hexagons fill bulb A. BLUE droplets stream in through its membrane from the bath. A gauge on bulb A rises above the zero line in AMBER, label 'Ψ_p up'.
scenes.narration: Put strong sugar solution in one bulb. The sugar lowers its water potential, so water rushes in by osmosis. The pressure inside rises.

scenes.tts: That pressure pushes the solution along the tube toward the other bulb. The sap flows in bulk, from higher pressure to lower.
scenes.visual: AMBER sap carrying GOLD hexagons slides along the tube from A to B. Bulb A's gauge is high, bulb B's low; an arrow labelled 'higher pressure to lower pressure' runs along the tube.
scenes.narration: That pressure pushes the solution along the tube toward the other bulb. The sap flows in bulk, from higher pressure to lower.

scenes.tts: In the plant, a leaf making sugar is the first bulb, the source. A root, a fruit or a shoot tip using sugar is the second bulb, a sink.
scenes.visual: Bulb A morphs into a mature leaf labelled 'source'; bulb B splits into a root, a fruit and a shoot tip, each labelled 'sink'. The AMBER tube becomes the phloem running between them.
scenes.narration: In the plant, a leaf making sugar is the first bulb, the source. A root, a fruit or a shoot tip using sugar is the second bulb, a sink.

scenes.tts: At a sink, sugar is removed, water leaves, and the pressure falls. The xylem alongside supplies the water at the source.
scenes.visual: At the root, GOLD hexagons are taken out of the AMBER tube into surrounding cells; BLUE droplets leave; the sink gauge drops (still above zero). At the leaf, BLUE droplets enter the AMBER tube from the neighbouring BLUE xylem line.
scenes.narration: At a sink, sugar is removed, water leaves, and the pressure falls. The xylem alongside supplies the water at the source.

scenes.tts: Sap flows from source to sink, wherever the sink sits. So it can run down to the roots or up to a growing shoot tip.
scenes.visual: From one source leaf halfway up the stem, two AMBER arrows set off: one down to the roots, one up to the shoot tip. Each sink has a low gauge; the leaf has a high one.
scenes.narration: Sap flows from source to sink, wherever the sink sits. So it can run down to the roots or up to a growing shoot tip.

scenes.tts: For decades there was an objection. Sieve tubes are narrow, and blocked at intervals by perforated end walls, the sieve plates. Pushing sap through metres of them seemed to need impossible pressures.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the AMBER tube: a chain of cells separated by end walls with small holes, labelled 'sieve plate'. A pressure dial labelled 'needed' spins toward a red zone marked 'impossible?'.
scenes.narration: For decades there was an objection. Sieve tubes are narrow, and blocked at intervals by perforated end walls, the sieve plates. Pushing sap through metres of them seemed to need impossible pressures.

scenes.tts: In two thousand sixteen, Michael Knoblauch, Michele Holbrook and colleagues tested this in the morning glory. They measured the pressure inside working sieve tubes with tiny probes.
scenes.caption: In 2016, Michael Knoblauch, Michele Holbrook and colleagues tested this in the morning glory. They measured the pressure inside working sieve tubes with tiny probes.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Knoblauch, Holbrook and colleagues, 2016: morning glory (Ipomoea nil)'. A climbing vine with trumpet flowers. A fine glass probe tip enters one AMBER sieve tube; a small gauge on it reads 'about 1.08 MPa (moderate-sized plants)'.
scenes.narration: In 2016, Michael Knoblauch, Michele Holbrook and colleagues tested this in the morning glory. They measured the pressure inside working sieve tubes with tiny probes.

scenes.tts: Then they made the sugar's path longer, by removing leaves from long vines. Now the sugar had to travel much farther to reach the roots.
scenes.visual: The vine stretches longer and longer; leaves near the base fade away, so the remaining source leaves sit far up the stem. A distance bar from source to root grows.
scenes.narration: Then they made the sugar's path longer, by removing leaves from long vines. Now the sugar had to travel much farther to reach the roots.

scenes.tts: With the same narrow tubes, the pressure needed would soar. If you make the path much longer, what must change for the sap still to arrive?
scenes.visual: The 'needed' dial from before spins up again as the vine grows. Question card: 'Longer path. What must change?'
scenes.narration: With the same narrow tubes, the pressure needed would soar. If you make the path much longer, what must change for the sap still to arrive?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Two things changed together. First, source pressure rose with path length. It passed two point two megapascals in the longest vine.
scenes.caption: Two things changed together. First, source pressure rose with path length. It passed 2.2 MPa in the longest vine.
scenes.visual: The source gauge climbs in AMBER as the vine lengthens, on-screen readings 'young plants: about 0.75 MPa' then 'longest vine: more than 2.2 MPa'.
scenes.narration: Two things changed together. First, source pressure rose with path length. It passed 2.2 MPa in the longest vine.

scenes.tts: Second, the tubes conducted five to six times better, mainly because the sieve-plate pores were wider. With both changes, the estimated reach of pressure flow matched the length of the vine.
scenes.visual: A sieve plate zooms in: its holes widen. A bar labelled 'sieve-tube conductivity' grows to '5 to 6 x'. Then an AMBER flow line extends to exactly the end of the vine, label 'estimated reach = vine length'.
scenes.narration: Second, the tubes conducted five to six times better, mainly because the sieve-plate pores were wider. With both changes, the estimated reach of pressure flow matched the length of the vine.

scenes.tts: That is one species, measured with care. The authors read it as strong support for pressure flow in this plant.
scenes.visual: A single morning glory vine sits on a card labelled 'one species: Ipomoea nil'. A check mark appears beside 'pressure flow' with the note 'strong support, this plant'.
scenes.narration: That is one species, measured with care. The authors read it as strong support for pressure flow in this plant.

scenes.tts: Where sugar goes in, water follows and the pressure rises. Sap is pushed to wherever sugar is taken out.
scenes.visual: Final diagram: source leaf with GOLD hexagons and BLUE droplets entering, AMBER gauge high; AMBER sap flowing to a root and a shoot tip with low gauges. The word 'pushed' in AMBER beside the flow; the first film's 'pulled' in RED beside the BLUE xylem.
scenes.narration: Where sugar goes in, water follows and the pressure rises. Sap is pushed to wherever sugar is taken out.

scenes.visual: Hex end card with one line only: 'Sugar in, water follows, pressure rises: sap is pushed to sinks.'
